title: Scriptorium: System Design and Implementation of a Multi-Human, Multi-AI Collaborative Digital Library Search Platform
summary: This technical report documents the design and implementation of Scriptorium, a digital library search interface designed to support multi-human, multi-AI collaboration: full cross-user transparency of search activity combined with a Manager--Worker architecture of seven role-specialized generative AI agents. A companion short demonstration paper describes Scriptorium's interaction design; because a demonstration format is constrained to a few pages, it necessarily omits most implementation detail. This report documents Scriptorium's complete system architecture, data model, collaborative-interaction design rationale, and AI orchestration mechanism, including verbatim agent prompts, the deterministic guardrails that constrain them, the language model and retrieval configuration, and the steps needed to run the system, so that the design can be inspected, critiqued, reproduced, and reused by other researchers. We also discuss the system's current limitations and the user study we are planning to evaluate its central hypothesis: that combining collaborative transparency with scoped multi-agent AI assistance increases serendipitous cross-pollination between collaborators' research threads.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Scriptorium, a reproducible digital-library search system for collaboration between multiple humans and seven role-specialized AI agents. It combines transparent sharing of search activity with a Manager–Worker orchestration architecture, and documents the system in detail for inspection, critique, and reuse. Its central hypothesis—that transparency plus scoped multi-agent assistance improves cross-pollination between research threads—remains to be evaluated in a planned user study.
AI.motivation: Existing demonstration papers often provide insufficient implementation detail for researchers to inspect, reproduce, or extend collaborative AI systems. Scriptorium is motivated by the need for a transparent, reusable infrastructure that supports both multi-person research collaboration and structured AI assistance, while addressing the possibility that collaborators miss useful connections between their separate research activities.
AI.method: The authors design and implement a digital-library search interface with full cross-user visibility of search activity and a Manager–Worker architecture coordinating seven role-specialized generative AI agents. The report specifies the system architecture, data model, interaction design rationale, agent prompts, deterministic guardrails, language-model and retrieval configurations, and deployment instructions. It also describes current limitations and outlines a planned user study to test the system’s central hypothesis.
AI.result: The primary result is a complete technical specification and implementation account of Scriptorium rather than an empirical evaluation. The report makes the system’s design and operating procedures available for inspection, reproduction, critique, and reuse. Evidence concerning whether the system improves research cross-pollination is not yet reported because the user study is planned rather than completed.
AI.conclusion: Scriptorium provides a transparent and reproducible platform for multi-human, multi-AI literature-search collaboration. Its proposed contribution is the integration of shared search visibility with scoped, role-based AI assistance. The effectiveness of this combination remains an open empirical question requiring the planned user study.

title: From AI-Free Gates to AI-First Work: How Engineering Students in India Navigate University Education and Campus Placements Without AI Guidelines
summary: Engineering graduates in India enter a technology sector that is being reshaped by generative AI, yet the route into that sector runs through examinations and campus placement screens that largely exclude AI. Institutions in India have an approved intake of nearly 2.9 million seats in engineering and technology for 2026-2027, but HCI research on how students prepare for AI-mediated work has drawn mostly on Western and East Asian settings. We interviewed 23 students and recent graduates of Indian engineering and computing programmes about how they used generative AI across coursework, examinations and placements, and how they judged their own readiness for work. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we report five themes, covering AI-first workplaces and AI-free placement screens, how participants prepared for placement, how they used AI in coursework, the role of faculty authority and enforcement, and participants' concerns about their readiness for work. Drawing on signaling theory, we discuss what grades and screen scores certify once AI can help produce them, and we offer recommendations for employers, institutions and AI tool designers.

AI.tldr: This study examines how Indian engineering students and recent graduates use generative AI in coursework, examinations, and job placements, and whether current assessment systems prepare or credibly signal readiness for AI-mediated work. Based on interviews with 23 participants and reflexive thematic analysis, it identifies tensions between AI-enabled workplaces and largely AI-free placement processes, along with concerns about the validity of grades and screening scores.
AI.motivation: Generative AI is rapidly changing technology work, but engineering education and recruitment systems may still assess students through processes that exclude or restrict AI. Existing HCI research has focused mainly on Western and East Asian contexts, leaving limited understanding of how students in India navigate AI use, institutional rules, faculty authority, and employment preparation. The study addresses this geographic and contextual gap while questioning whether conventional academic and recruitment signals remain meaningful when AI contributes to performance.
AI.method: The researchers conducted qualitative interviews with 23 students and recent graduates from Indian engineering and computing programmes. Participants discussed their use of generative AI in coursework, examinations, and placement preparation, as well as their perceptions of workplace readiness. The data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis, producing five themes: the contrast between AI-enabled workplaces and AI-free placement screens; preparation for placements; AI use in coursework; faculty authority and enforcement; and concerns about readiness for work. Signaling theory provided the conceptual lens for interpreting the meaning of grades and screening scores.
AI.result: The findings reveal a mismatch between participants’ anticipated AI-mediated workplaces and recruitment systems that largely prohibit or omit AI. Participants used generative AI in educational contexts, but their practices were shaped by faculty rules, institutional enforcement, and concerns about legitimacy. The study also finds uncertainty about whether grades and placement scores accurately represent individual competence once AI can assist in producing assessed outputs. Participants consequently expressed concerns about their preparedness for actual work, despite succeeding in conventional academic or recruitment systems.
AI.conclusion: The paper argues that institutions and employers should reconsider assessment, placement, and skill-signaling practices in light of generative AI. Academic and recruitment systems need clearer, more realistic approaches to evaluating AI-supported competence rather than relying solely on AI-free performance measures. The authors provide recommendations for employers, educational institutions, and AI tool designers to better align preparation and evaluation with contemporary technology work.

title: A Stratified Multi-Rater Evaluation of LLM-Based Virtual Standardized Patients with a Deployed Data-Generation Platform
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets. 39 pages (10 pages of main text), 3 figures and 3 tables in the main text, 4 figures and 4 tables in the appendices. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/nwirandx/Korean-OSCE-history-taking-dialogues Code: https://github.com/JINAILAB/OSCE-SimBench
summary: The Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) is widely used to assess clinical communication skills in medical education, requiring trainees to take histories and reason clinically with standardized patients (SPs). Large language model (LLM)-based virtual standardized patients (VSPs), typically built by persona-injected prompting, offer a practical alternative. However, existing evaluations rely on a single backbone LLM, small human rater panels, or LLM-as-a-judge scoring without an utterance-aligned human-expert reference, and so cannot identify the specific shortcomings of individual models. We evaluated four LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama-3.1 70B, and HyperCLOVA X), spanning commercial, open-source and Korean-developed models, against a human-expert reference across three Korean OSCE cases (hematuria, fever in pregnancy, and chronic cough). In a double-blind, fully crossed design, 17 senior medical-student raters scored every model utterance on three sentence-level and six encounter-level Likert metrics, yielding 7,480 data points. We analyzed the scores using a stratified linear mixed-effects model based on an 11-category history-taking and 3-level linguistic-form taxonomy. At the encounter level, three of the four LLMs fell 0.08 to 0.47 Likert points below the human-expert reference on Comprehensibility, Consistency and Hallucination-freeness. The difference was not statistically significant for Hallucination-freeness in Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o, Consistency in GPT-4o, and Engagement in HyperCLOVA X. Llama-3.1 70B fell significantly below the reference on all six metrics. We also introduce a web-based OSCE platform that supports virtual practice across diverse clinical cases and continuously collects student-VSP dialogues under research and privacy consent.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks four LLM-based virtual standardized patients against a human-expert reference in Korean OSCE communication tasks using utterance-level human ratings and mixed-effects analysis. GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet performed closest to the reference on most dimensions, HyperCLOVA X showed a relative engagement strength, and Llama-3.1 70B underperformed significantly across all encounter-level metrics. The authors also provide a privacy-consented web platform for virtual OSCE practice and dialogue data collection.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM-based virtual standardized patients are limited by single-model comparisons, small human-rater samples, or LLM-based judging without utterance-aligned expert references. These limitations make it difficult to determine which models have specific communication or clinical-response weaknesses. The study therefore seeks a rigorous, human-grounded comparison across commercially developed, open-source, and Korean-developed LLMs in realistic OSCE cases.
AI.method: Four LLMs—GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama-3.1 70B, and HyperCLOVA X—were evaluated in three Korean OSCE scenarios: hematuria, fever during pregnancy, and chronic cough. In a double-blind, fully crossed design, 17 senior medical students rated every model utterance and the human-expert reference. Ratings covered three sentence-level and six encounter-level Likert metrics. The authors analyzed 7,480 observations with a stratified linear mixed-effects model organized around 11 history-taking categories and three linguistic-form levels. They also developed a web-based OSCE platform that enables virtual practice and consented collection of student–VSP dialogues.
AI.result: At the encounter level, three models scored 0.08–0.47 Likert points below the human reference on Comprehensibility, Consistency, and Hallucination-freeness. Differences were not statistically significant for Hallucination-freeness in Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o, Consistency in GPT-4o, or Engagement in HyperCLOVA X. Llama-3.1 70B scored significantly below the reference on all six encounter-level metrics. Overall, GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet most closely approached expert performance, while HyperCLOVA X showed comparatively strong engagement and Llama-3.1 70B exhibited the broadest deficits.
AI.conclusion: Human-expert, utterance-aligned evaluation reveals model-specific strengths and weaknesses that aggregate or LLM-judge evaluations may miss. GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet appear most suitable among the tested systems for Korean OSCE-style VSP use, although neither fully matches the expert reference on every metric. The proposed platform may support scalable practice and longitudinal research, but broader validation across cases, raters, languages, clinical specialties, and safety outcomes is still needed.

title: VIRA-Bench: Diagnosing Pedagogical Contingency Understanding in Online Tutoring Videos
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Main Conference (Oral). 21 pages
summary: Understanding a one-to-one tutoring video requires more than recognizing its events. A model must connect a visible teacher intervention to the learner response it elicits and to the follow-up adjusted to that response. Existing video and educational-dialogue benchmarks typically emphasize event recognition, temporal reasoning, social-state inference, or transcript-based interaction, but rarely diagnose this action-response-adjustment relation. We introduce VIRA-Bench, a focused diagnostic benchmark for short-horizon pedagogical contingency in one-to-one online tutoring. VIRA-Bench contains 1,005 tutoring clips and 1,322 multiple-choice questions with researcher evidence audit and expert verification, organized into Observable Evidence Grounding (OEG), Interaction Contingency Reasoning (ICR), and Support-Response Modeling (SRM). Across 11 models, the best reaches 61.3%, well below the 91.0% human reference on a stratified subset, and ICR generally has the lowest layer accuracy among leading models. Under controlled input manipulations, removing video most strongly degrades OEG, whereas disrupting temporal order most strongly degrades ICR. Free-response, Stem+Options, and synchronized-shuffle controls show that response format, static question cues, and video-ASR mismatch do not explain these layer-specific patterns. The results identify distinct behavioral evidence dependencies without claiming an internal architectural mechanism. VIRA-Bench provides a focused evaluation resource for multimodal dialogue grounding, pedagogical discourse, and temporal reasoning in online tutoring.

AI.tldr: VIRA-Bench is a diagnostic benchmark for evaluating whether multimodal models can understand short-horizon pedagogical contingency in one-to-one tutoring videos: linking teacher actions to learner responses and subsequent instructional adjustments. It includes 1,005 clips and 1,322 verified multiple-choice questions across evidence grounding, contingency reasoning, and support-response modeling. Model performance remains substantially below humans, with interaction contingency reasoning as the main weakness.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks commonly evaluate event recognition, temporal reasoning, social-state inference, or transcript-based educational interaction, but they rarely test whether a system can determine how a teacher's intervention produces a learner response and how the teacher then adapts. The paper addresses this gap by targeting pedagogical contingency as a distinct and diagnostically measurable capability in online tutoring videos.
AI.method: The authors construct VIRA-Bench from 1,005 one-to-one tutoring clips and 1,322 multiple-choice questions. Questions are organized into three layers: Observable Evidence Grounding (OEG), Interaction Contingency Reasoning (ICR), and Support-Response Modeling (SRM). Researcher evidence audits and expert verification support dataset quality. They evaluate 11 models against a 91.0% human reference on a stratified subset. Controlled manipulations remove video, disrupt temporal order, alter response format, provide static question cues, and test video-ASR synchronization to identify which evidence types affect performance.
AI.result: The strongest model achieves only 61.3%, substantially below the 91.0% human reference. ICR is generally the weakest layer among leading models. Removing video most harms OEG, while disrupting temporal order most harms ICR. Free-response, Stem+Options, and synchronized-shuffle controls indicate that response format, static wording cues, and video-ASR mismatch do not account for the observed layer-specific patterns.
AI.conclusion: VIRA-Bench reveals a substantial gap between current multimodal models and humans in understanding pedagogical action-response-adjustment sequences. Its controlled results support distinct behavioral dependencies on visual evidence and temporal order, while avoiding claims about specific internal model mechanisms. The benchmark is useful for research on multimodal dialogue grounding, pedagogical discourse, and temporal reasoning in tutoring.

title: The Serendiptionnaire: a Questionnaire for Measuring Experienced Serendipity
summary: Serendipity is important to design for, yet it remains difficult to measure and evaluate. No validated questionnaire exists, so studies either borrow ResQue's novelty scale, which does not measure serendipity, or build their own items, which makes findings hard to compare and synthesize. Building on our earlier conceptualization of experienced serendipity as a fortuitous encounter with content that is both refreshing and enriching, we developed the Serendiptionnaire, a questionnaire that operationalizes our framework. We conducted twenty-seven cognitive interviews over three iterations with respondents who varied in age, education level, country of birth, and English proficiency, while they browsed recommendations on platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, and Spotify. After each iteration, we revised the items until respondents interpreted them as intended. The resulting instrument consists of modular scales that researchers can combine to target the specific flavor of serendipity they want to study or design for. The Serendiptionnaire offers a ground truth for validating system-centered serendipity metrics and LLM-based evaluations, and it provides a nuanced evaluation of users' experienced serendipity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces and refines the Serendiptionnaire, a modular questionnaire designed to validly measure users’ experienced serendipity when encountering recommended content.
AI.motivation: Serendipity is valuable in recommender-system design but lacks a validated measurement instrument. Existing studies often misuse ResQue’s novelty scale or create incomparable custom items, limiting reliable evaluation and synthesis across studies.
AI.method: The authors operationalize experienced serendipity as a fortuitous encounter with content that is both refreshing and enriching. They conducted 27 cognitive interviews across three iterative rounds with demographically and linguistically diverse participants while they browsed recommendations on Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, and Spotify. Items were revised after each round based on how respondents interpreted them.
AI.result: The final Serendiptionnaire consists of modular scales that can be combined to measure different forms or dimensions of serendipity. Iterative cognitive testing improved the alignment between item wording and the intended conceptual framework.
AI.conclusion: The instrument provides a more appropriate and nuanced measure of users’ experienced serendipity. It can serve as a reference standard for validating system-centered serendipity metrics and LLM-based evaluations, while supporting comparable research and design evaluation.

title: Measurement-Guided Conversion of Laboratory Eye-Tracking Data for VR Authentication
summary: Eye-movement authentication in virtual reality (VR) needs longitudinal training data, yet most such datasets come from lab trackers. We convert lab recordings to a VR headset's signal quality while keeping their eye movement, using only unpaired VR recordings of other people. Measurements show that the headset's added noise dominates above 7.8 Hz and that its quality is consistent within a person. A parametric device model re-creates the headset's sampling, a person-consistent calibration error and spectrally shaped noise, and a frequency-locked diffusion renderer re-textures that high-frequency noise. Converted GazeBase recordings match GazeBaseVR in noise level and accuracy, keep their source's saccade dynamics, and are harder to tell from real VR data than two prior conversions. An authenticator trained only on converted data verifies unseen VR users at a 5.9% equal error rate with 45 s of gaze, close to real VR training (5.8%); with 5 s, a gap remains.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a data-conversion framework that transforms laboratory eye-tracking recordings into realistic VR-headset gaze data without paired recordings, enabling longitudinal VR eye-movement authentication training. The method models device sampling, person-consistent calibration error, and frequency-shaped noise, then uses a frequency-locked diffusion model to render realistic high-frequency noise. Converted data closely match real VR data, preserve saccade dynamics, improve realism over prior methods, and support authentication performance nearly equal to training on real VR data when 45 seconds of gaze is available.
AI.motivation: VR eye-movement authentication requires substantial longitudinal data, but existing long-term datasets are primarily collected with laboratory eye trackers rather than consumer VR headsets. Directly collecting equivalent VR data is costly, and naive domain conversion may distort biometric eye-movement dynamics or fail to reproduce headset-specific noise. The paper therefore aims to generate realistic VR-like recordings from existing lab data using only unpaired VR recordings from other users.
AI.method: The authors first characterize the VR headset's measurement properties, finding that added device noise dominates above 7.8 Hz and that signal quality is relatively consistent for each individual. They construct a parametric device model that reproduces headset sampling, person-consistent calibration error, and spectrally shaped noise. A frequency-locked diffusion renderer then synthesizes realistic high-frequency noise while preserving the original eye-movement signal. The framework converts GazeBase recordings into VR-like data using unpaired recordings from other people for model learning.
AI.result: The converted recordings match GazeBaseVR in noise level and accuracy while preserving the source recordings' saccade dynamics. They are more difficult to distinguish from real VR recordings than outputs from two prior conversion methods. An authenticator trained only on converted data achieves a 5.9% equal error rate with 45 seconds of gaze from unseen VR users, close to the 5.8% EER obtained with real VR training. With only 5 seconds of gaze, a performance gap remains.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that physically and statistically grounded conversion can effectively bridge laboratory eye-tracking data and VR-headset data for authentication. The near-equivalent 45-second authentication performance indicates that converted data can substantially reduce the need for large, longitudinal VR collections, although short-duration authentication still requires further improvement.
